Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Anya, a 28-year-old tax consultant, had been referred for therapy after her GP noticed her increasing withdrawal and physical complaints. Her journey to this point began just over a year ago, with an experience that fractured her sense of safety. She had been on a solo trip exploring a vibrant market in a country she’d always dreamed of visiting when she was suddenly grabbed and pulled into a nondescript van. The next 72 hours were a blur of terror, confined to a small, windowless room, never knowing who would enter or when, subjected to degrading searches and threats that left her feeling utterly dehumanized. The memory of the rough hands, the cold floor, and the constant, gnawing fear of what might happen next was seared into her mind. Eventually, she was released, disoriented and traumatized, with no explanation or apology. The authorities had been unable to identify her captors, offering little comfort or hope for justice.

Back home in her American apartment, the world felt fundamentally altered. What frightened her most now was the unexpected. A colleague walking quickly past her cubicle in the open-plan office could send a jolt of adrenaline through her, her body reacting as if a new threat had materialized. The sudden movement, even if peripheral, would cause her to flinch violently, her heart pounding. She found herself instinctively positioning her chair so that her back was always against the wall, allowing her a full, unobstructed view of the room. It was the only way she felt she could monitor her surroundings, a habit that made her feel constantly on edge but also paradoxically safer. When clients came into her office, she found herself scanning their movements, unable to fully relax until they were seated and still. At home, the vigilance intensified. Sleep was elusive, punctuated by her hyper-alertness to every creak and groan of the old building. She spent hours listening, straining to discern any sound that might mean someone was entering her home, convinced that the quiet hum of the refrigerator or the rustle of leaves outside her window could mask a more sinister approach.

The emotional scars ran deep, manifesting as a pervasive sense of shame and injustice. Anya had come to believe that the event happened because of the way she acted. She replayed every moment leading up to her abduction, convinced that if she had taken a different street, worn different clothes, or simply been more aware, it wouldn’t have happened. This self-blame was a constant, corrosive whisper in her mind. Compounding this was the bitter reality that the people responsible had faced no consequences. The lack of accountability infuriated her and left her feeling as though the world was an inherently dangerous place where evil went unpunished. But perhaps the most profound wound was the deep body shame she carried. The memories of the degrading searches, the feeling of her personal space being utterly violated, made her feel profoundly uncomfortable in her own skin. She avoided looking at herself in the mirror, dressed in loose, concealing clothes, and recoiled from even innocent physical touch, feeling as though her body was no longer her own, but a site of past violation.

Over the past year, these internal battles had begun to carve visible lines in her life. Her preference for sitting with her back to the wall made team meetings awkward, as she’d subtly rearrange chairs or choose seats that afforded her this sense of security, sometimes leading to minor friction with colleagues who didn’t understand her rigidity. Her constant vigilance made it difficult to focus on complex tax documents, leading to errors that she’d then obsess over, further fueling her self-blame. Social invitations dwindled, as she found the effort of constantly monitoring open spaces and managing her startle response exhausting. She stopped going to the gym, unable to bear the thought of changing in the locker room or feeling exposed in group classes. Her once vibrant social life had shrunk to almost nothing, leaving her isolated in her apartment, where her intrusion monitoring became even more intense. The cumulative toll on her professional performance and personal well-being had become undeniable. The fear of an unknown sound, the sudden flash of movement, or the feeling of an open space had become her constant companions, slowly eroding her life. It was the realization that her life was becoming smaller and smaller, dictated by these unseen threats, that finally prompted her to seek professional help, desperate for a way to reclaim some semblance of the person she once was.
